header.tag_why: The CFO's decision turned when Wen priced her manual matching hours and unmatched-deposit write-offs from her own statements ('that's my number, not yours'), after which 'it was paperwork'; the reconciliation capability is what made that number possible.

messaging_changes.current_line: Financial infrastructure to grow globally, in every currency.
messaging_changes.change: For finance buyers at domestic B2B sellers and invoice-driven businesses (distributors), open with M9 in their words instead of the global-infrastructure line: 'Know where every deposit came from, and close month-end without a week of archaeology.' Avoid 'infrastructure' and 'payments'; say 'deposits' and 'month-end'. Follow straight into the payout-to-transaction-to-ERP demo.
messaging_changes.why: The M1 opener met 'Silence', the buyer never said 'payments' or 'infrastructure' and talked about 'the deposits' and 'I just want to know where my money is', so an opener built on her words and the reconciliation outcome fits her better than ours.

messaging_changes.current_line: Proven ROI, backed by an independent economic impact study.
messaging_changes.change: For CFOs and finance buyers, lead the value proof with a reconciliation cost workup built from one month of the customer's own statements (manual matching hours plus unmatched-deposit write-offs), offered right after the reconciliation demo: 'Send us one month of statements and we'll price what month-end costs you today.' Keep the independent study as backup, not the main proof.
messaging_changes.why: The deal went from 'I had it at 20 percent' to signed after the rep priced the CFO's pain from her own statements, which she valued because 'that's my number, not yours.'

messaging_changes.current_line: Built for developers: launch payments fast with our APIs, docs and sandbox.
messaging_changes.change: Stop leading with the developer story when the economic buyer is in finance. Keep APIs, docs and sandbox in a technical appendix for the IT contact, and put the close or reconciliation outcome in finance terms on page one of any proposal that may reach a CFO.
messaging_changes.why: The developer story 'went nowhere', and the first proposal, written around portal, checkout and APIs, was rejected on page one by the CFO who decided the deal.

messaging_changes.change: Add a distributor or wholesale customer story with a reference call that finance buyers can take. Use it in place of retail and software stories when selling to distributors and wholesalers.
messaging_changes.why: Our existing customer stories were dismissed with 'this is a company that sells sweaters', and the buyer raised the missing distributor reference twice even though she signed.

trigger.insight: The inbound described IT's project, a reorder portal. The money and the urgency sat with a new CFO whose first close took nine days of hand-matching deposits, processor statements and ERP invoices. The rep only found this on the third call, so the deal's real trigger never appeared in the inbound.
trigger.messaging: For distributors and other invoice-driven businesses, qualify for the finance pain early (days to close, manual deposit matching) and lead with M9 even when the inbound asks about checkout.

decider.insight: The rep's day-to-day contact said outright that he could only recommend. Even so, the first proposal was written to his problem (portal, checkout, APIs). It stalled for three weeks because the decider rejected it on page one. Proposals are being read by an economic buyer the deck was never written for.
decider.messaging: Page one of any proposal that may reach a CFO should state the close or reconciliation outcome in finance terms, with checkout and APIs moved to an appendix.

competitor.insight: There is no evidence of a real competitive pitch. The bank's only reported defense was offering to look at rates, and that annoyed a buyer whose problem was reconciliation, not price. Her one new question afterwards was about a named contact, because her bank rep had changed and she didn't know who the new one was. That suggests the incumbent relationship was weaker than a bank bundle usually is.
competitor.messaging: Against bank-bundled incumbents, don't compete on rates; position a named contact and the reconciliation outcome, and note that M5's tiered response times don't speak to the named-person need she raised.

message.insight: M1 (global, every currency) and M2 (developers) both missed. This is a business selling to restaurants in three states, with a four-person IT team running an off-the-shelf portal. The only unprompted buyer reaction in the whole deal was to the payout-to-transaction-to-ERP demo (M9). She asked to see it with her own data right away, which shows the demo created the demand for proof.
message.messaging: For domestic B2B sellers, replace the M1 opener and the M2 developer story with an M9-led reconciliation demo and an offer to run it on their statements.

decided.insight: The deal went from a rep-estimated 20 percent to paperwork in a single meeting. The deciding artifact was a cost-of-doing-nothing figure built from the customer's statements, staff costs and write-offs. The CFO explicitly valued it because it was not ours. The exact figure isn't known; the rep remembers it only as low six figures a year.
decided.messaging: Lead with a statement-based reconciliation cost workup using the customer's own hours and write-offs, and present M6's independent study as backup, not the main proof.

gaps.insight: We had no wholesale or distributor reference. M8's retail and software stories were dismissed on sight, and she raised the missing reference twice. Unified counter-plus-online reporting for 14 branches was asserted from a slide, not demoed. That claim is still unproven with this customer and could surface at rollout.
gaps.messaging: Build a distributor or wholesale customer story with a reference call, and back M3 claims about counter sales landing in the same report with a live demo rather than a slide.

language.insight: The buyer's words are about visibility and cash (where the money is, deposits, month-end). Our words are about payments and infrastructure, which she never used. Her IT contact talked about the processor, so finance and IT vocabularies differ even inside the account.
language.messaging: Rewrite M9 for finance buyers in their terms: know where every deposit came from and close month-end without the 'week of archaeology', with no mention of infrastructure.

gaps.question: What was the exact dollar figure in Wen's cost workup, and how much of it was write-offs versus staff hours?
gaps.follow_up: Ask Wen for the workup file and the method, so it can become a reusable template.

gaps.question: What, if anything, did Fiserv or the bank show beyond offering to review rates?
gaps.follow_up: Ask Paul (or Ines at a check-in) whether the bank made any proposal or counter-offer after she said they were looking around.

gaps.question: Was any other provider evaluated besides staying with the incumbent?
gaps.follow_up: Ask Dana whether Paul or Ines mentioned any other vendor during the evaluation.

gaps.question: Did the named-contact answer weigh in the decision, and what does she expect from it?
gaps.follow_up: Ask Ines in an onboarding check-in what she expects from a named contact and how it compared to her bank relationship.

gaps.question: Is the branch counter-sales reporting in the signed scope, and does it work as shown on the slide?
gaps.follow_up: Ask Dana and Wen whether the 14 branches' card readers are in the contract and when the same-report view will be demoed or delivered.

close.rep_takeaway: Dana's deal was saved by a demo that put a price on the CFO's own pain, not by the pitch. The month lost on the portal could have been avoided by asking early who owns the cost of the problem and pricing it in their own numbers. When a contact says 'I can recommend, she decides,' write the proposal for her.
